Early‑dark‑energy (EDE) models try to raise the inferred value of the Hubble constant by adding a new, short‑lived component that contributes to the energy density of the Universe just before recombination.  By increasing the pre‑recombination expansion rate, the sound horizon at last scattering is reduced, which allows the CMB to be fit with a larger \(H_{0}\) while keeping the angular scale of the acoustic peaks fixed [1][2].  The most studied incarnation is the “standard” EDE model, in which a scalar field with a potential that temporarily dominates the energy budget at a redshift \(z\sim 10^{3}\) is introduced; variants include phase‑transition EDE, AdS‑EDE, and inverse‑power‑law EDE [2][3].

Observational tests, however, place strong limits on how much extra energy can be added without spoiling the excellent agreement of the ΛCDM model with the CMB temperature and polarization spectra, the baryon‑acoustic‑oscillation (BAO) scale, and large‑scale structure.  Fits to the combined CMB+BAO+SN+local‑\(H_{0}\) data show that the EDE contribution must be small enough that the best‑fit \(H_{0}\) is only modestly higher (e.g. \(H_{0}\sim70.2\) km s\(^{-1}\) Mpc\(^{-1}\) for an inverse‑power‑law EDE with index \(n=10\)) and that the model still reproduces the observed CMB power spectra and matter‑power spectrum [3].  Moreover, the required fine‑tuning of the scalar‑field potential and the tight correlation with other cosmological parameters (e.g. the spectral index and the baryon density) mean that EDE models often introduce new tensions or degrade the fit to other data sets [1][4].
